Chelm Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Chełm, Poland

Demolished. This record shows a tension worth noting: it is categorized as 'fenced and protected,' yet the source's demolished field marks it as 'yes.' Chełm's Jewish community, present from the second half of the 15th century, appears in historical records as a kehilla paying crown tax by 1507, and comprised about 45 percent of the city's population by 1939. This cemetery likely dates to the late 15th century; a matzevah discovered in 2019 bears the date 1514. During WWII, German occupying forces forced Jews to remove matzevot and use them to pave roads, sidewalks, and courtyards in front of offices and police headquarters; the cemetery also became a citywide site of individual and mass executions and burials, and tombstone theft by local residents continued well after the war. In 1994, funded by the Nissenbaum family, most of the cemetery was fenced, though an eastern section is now occupied by a petrol station. Since 1995, descendants of Chełm's Jews have erected their own memorial stelae in the cemetery's northern section to commemorate their families — a practice that continues today, though it does not align with regulations set by the Rabbinic Committee of Cemeteries, a tension the record itself notes.
